"O phantom of Hind, you have left me sleepless, when you came to us by night while the night had grown dark."

The root of ghasaq is flowing with harm. It is derived from the saying "ghasaqat al-qurhah" when its pus flows. Al-Ghassaq is the pus of the people of Hell, because it flows with torment. "Ghasaqat 'aynuhu" means that his eye's tears flowed painfully into the throat.

Accordingly, if the darkness is the night, then in the phrase ﴿when it settles﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: when it becomes dark. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: when it enters. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: when it departs. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: when it is still. This was said by al-Yaman ibn Ri'ab.

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. The people of interpretation (Ahl al-Ta'wil) said: these are female sorcerers who blow into the knots of threads for magic. A poet said:

"I seek refuge in my Lord from the blowing of the blowers, the deceivers of the deceptive kind."

Some people do something similar in incantations, seeking healing, as Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah said:

"I blew into a thread, like an incantation, out of fear of the jinn and the envious."

Al-Hasan related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever ties a knot and then blows into it has practised magic, and whoever practises magic has committed shirk, and whoever attaches himself to something will be left to it." [p. 376]

Nafth is blowing into knots without saliva, and tafl is blowing into them with saliva. Regarding ﴿the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ there are three aspects:

One: it is the creation of illusion of harm and the imagining of sickness without it having any real effect on harm or sickness, except a feeling that may sadden, or harmful food that may reach the body by a hidden trick.

The second: one may be harmed by a sickness caused by an accidental emission that separates and then attaches itself to the bewitched person and affects him, like the effect of the evil eye, and just as from the mouth of one who yawns there emerges something that causes a similar effect in the one facing him.

The third: this may happen through the help of servant jinn, by which God tests some of His servants.

As for what is related about the bewitching of the Prophet (ﷺ), most of them affirmed it: that a group of Jews bewitched him and threw the knot of his magic into a well, until God revealed it to him there.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) fell ill with a severe ailment, and while he was between sleep and wakefulness, two angels came to him, one at his head and the other at his feet. One of them said: What is his ailment? The other said: He has been bewitched (mathbub, meaning magicked). Tabb means magic. He asked: Who bewitched him? He said: Labid ibn al-A'sam the Jew. He had thrown it into the well of Dharwan under a rock in it. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent 'Ammar ibn Yasir, who extracted the magic from it. It is related that it contained eleven knots. He ordered the knots to be untied, and every time a knot was untied he felt relief, until all the knots were untied. It was as if he had been released from a tether. Then the two surahs were revealed to him, and they are eleven verses, corresponding to the number of knots, and he was commanded to seek refuge with them." Others denied this and refused to attribute it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), even if it is authentic concerning others, because of what it would imply of continued derangement of his intellect. God, the Exalted, also rejected those who said of His Messenger: ﴿You follow none but a man bewitched﴾ (Qur'an 17:47).

﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾. As for envy (hasad), it is the wish for the removal of the blessing of the envied person, even if the envier does not obtain the like of it. Competition (munafasah) is the wish for the like of it without the blessing being removed. So envy is a blameworthy evil, whereas competition is a permissible desire. It has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The believer desires good for others, and the hypocrite envies." Regarding seeking refuge from the evil of an envier when he envies there are two aspects:

One: from the evil of his self and his eye, for he may afflict with it, causing harm and injury. The one afflicted by the evil eye is called ma'yun. A poet said:

"Your people used to consider you a leader, and I think you are a leader afflicted by the evil eye."

The second: that the excess of envy may drive him to inflict harm on the envied person, for he follows faults and seeks slips. It has been said that envy was the first sin by which God was disobeyed in heaven and on earth. Iblis envied Adam until he expelled him from the Garden. On earth, Qabil the son of Adam envied his brother Habil until he killed him. We seek refuge in God from the evil from which He has commanded us to seek refuge.

The surah opens with "Say" (qul) because God commanded His Prophet to say it, and it is part of the surah since it was revealed together with it. Some eloquent early scholars said: "Memorise the qalaqil" (the words that cause tremors or repetitions). On this there are two interpretations:

One: say "qul" in every surah that begins with it, because it is part of it.

The second: memorise the surah that begins with "qul" so as to affirm it by the command to recite it.

**Surah al-Falaq (The Daybreak)**

Makki according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir, and Madani according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

This surah and al-Nas are the two "Mu'awwidhatan" (the two seeking refuge) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), revealed when the Jews bewitched him. It was also said that the two surahs were called "al-Muqashqishatan" (the two that cleanse), meaning that they clear one of hypocrisy. Ibn Mas'ud claimed that they are a supplication for seeking refuge and are not part of the Qur'an. This is an opinion that contradicts the consensus (ijma') of the Companions and the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt).

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. On this there are six interpretations: [p. 374]

The first: al-Falaq is a prison in Hell. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is one of the names of Hell. This was said by Abu 'Abd al-Rahman.

The third: it is the whole of creation. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: it is the cleaving of dawn. This was said by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"O night that I did not sleep through, I spent it reclining, watching the stars until the daybreak lit up."

The fifth: it refers to mountains and rocks that split open with water.

The sixth: it is everything that splits open to bring forth all that is created: animals, the dawn, grain and date-stones, and every plant and other thing. This was said by al-Hasan.

The people of subtle meanings (Ashab al-Ghawamid) say that it means the cleaving of hearts to understanding, until understanding reaches them and enters them. The root of falaq is a wide split. It is said that dawn is called falaq because the darkness is split away from it, just as it is called fajr because light bursts forth from it.

﴿From the evil of what He created﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: the evil of what He created is Hell. This was said by Thabit al-Banani.

The second: Iblis and his offspring. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: the evil of what He created in this world and the Hereafter. This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

Regarding this evil there are two aspects:

One: it is to be understood in its general sense, covering every kind of evil.

The second: it is specific to the evil for which the one afflicted by it deserves reward.

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. On this there are four interpretations. The first: it means the sun when it sets. This was said by Ibn Shihab.

The second: the moon when it enters, that is, enters into darkness. Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman related from 'A'ishah that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) took my hand, then looked at the moon and said: O 'A'ishah, seek refuge in God from the evil of the darkness when it settles, for this is the darkness when it settles."
